bib.title: Learning LangChain, Chapter 11. Building with LLMs

question: How should LLMs be put in the hands of end users, given that conventional palette-and-canvas interfaces assume capabilities known ahead of time?
contributions: Three UX patterns for LLM applications (interactive chatbot, collaborative editing, ambient computing), each with the components needed to build it

results.claim: Streaming chat may become the command line of the LLM era, a niche interface closest to direct programming access.

limits: No experiments or measurements; patterns are asserted, and the authors say these are not the only ones and the dust will take a while to settle.
The chapter lists components but gives no implementation, code or evaluation.
practices: Chatbot minimum: a chat model plus conversation history (Interactive Chatbots).
Add streaming output, token by token or in larger chunks, to hide latency (Interactive Chatbots).
Expose canvas operations as tools, e.g. 'get selected text' and 'insert text at end of doc' (Interactive Chatbots).
Add human-in-the-loop confirmation or editing once tools can change the canvas (Interactive Chatbots).

Collaborative agent needs six things: shared state, task manager, merging forks (manual or CRDT/OT), concurrency (interrupt, cancel, reroute, queue), undo/redo stack, intermediate output (Collaborative Editing).
Ambient agent needs five things: triggers, long-term memory, reflection, summarised output, task manager (Ambient Computing).
Build something rough, talk to users and iterate (Summary).

terms.definition: Only one user edits the document at a time before passing it on; example Microsoft Office.
Multiple editors work simultaneously and unaware of each other, with merge strategies and conflict resolution; example Git/GitHub.
Multiple editors work on the same document at once, seeing each other's changes; example Google Docs.
A step in which the LLM updates its long-term memory, possibly modifying its internal rules for detecting future interesting events.
Always-on background software that pipes up when something interesting has happened.
